quiz.title: Module 3 — Understanding Images
quiz.description: Monday's quiz covers pixels and raster formats, bit depth and posterization, the difference between 8-bit and 16-bit documents, why converting a JPEG to 16-bit adds no colour, and the role of a background and adjustment layers in Photoshop.

questions.prompt: What are the tiny squares that make up a raster image called?
options: Vectors
Pixels
Layers
Gradients
questions.explanation: A raster image is a grid of pixels, each holding a colour value. Vectors describe shapes mathematically instead, which is why they scale without losing quality.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a common raster image file format mentioned in the transcript?
options: SVG
AI
EPS
PNG
questions.explanation: PNG is a raster format. SVG, AI and EPS are vector formats, so they are not built from a pixel grid.

questions.prompt: What does bit depth refer to in a raster image?
options: The amount of colour information available in the file
The physical width and height of the image
The number of adjustment layers in Photoshop
The size of the image on a computer screen
questions.explanation: Bit depth is how many bits describe each pixel's colour, which sets how many distinct colours the file can hold — not its dimensions.

questions.prompt: What is posterization in image editing?
options: An increase in the number of colours in an image
A process of enlarging an image without changing its colours
A decrease in apparent bit depth that causes poor colour transitions
A technique for converting raster images into vector graphics
questions.explanation: Posterization shows up as banding in a gradient: the file no longer has enough colour steps, so smooth blends break into visible stripes.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements about 8-bit and 16-bit images are correct?
options: An 8-bit document can display about 16.8 million colours.
A 16-bit image can store fewer colours than an 8-bit image.
A 16-bit image can display trillions of colours.
An 8-bit image always provides more editing flexibility than a 16-bit image.
questions.explanation: Both A and C are correct: 8-bit gives roughly 16.8 million colours, while 16-bit reaches into the trillions. More bits means more editing headroom before banding appears.

questions.prompt: Why does converting an existing JPEG image from 8-bit to 16-bit provide no additional colour information?
options: JPEG images cannot be opened in Photoshop.
The colour information was already limited when the image was saved as an 8-bit JPEG.
JPEG images contain only black and white pixels.
Photoshop automatically removes all colour information from JPEG images.
questions.explanation: Changing the bit depth of a file cannot restore data that was discarded at capture or save. The extra bits are empty headroom, not recovered colour.

questions.prompt: What is one important purpose of a background in graphic design?
options: To compete with the main text and design elements
To eliminate the need for typography
To make every element equally noticeable
To provide a foundation and establish the environment for other design elements
questions.explanation: A background sets the environment the design sits in and gives the other elements something to rest on. It should support the hierarchy, not compete with it.

questions.prompt: Which Photoshop feature allows designers to combine images and create unique backgrounds?
options: Adjustment Layers
Text Alignment
Page Margins
Paragraph Spacing
questions.explanation: Adjustment layers apply colour and tone changes without altering the underlying pixels, which is what makes combining images into a background controllable.
